analytic.title: Response-Time Analysis for Non-Preemptive Scheduling in Multi-Core Systems with Shared Resources

div.p: There is an important class of scheduling strategies that has not been sufficiently covered by the real-time scheduling literature. The new multi-core extensions of the AUTOSAR automotive standard -the dominating automotive design worldwide -uses a combination of partitioned fixed-priority scheduling strategies with preemptive and non-preemptive execution and (potentially) arbitrary deadlines. Since multi-core systems in general use shared resources, this leads to the problem of analyzing preemptive and non-preemptive multiprocessor scheduling with shared resources. While preemptive scheduling has been well investigated in this setup, non-preemptive scheduling analysis is still open and cannot simply be derived. In this paper, we address this subject and present an analysis method which allows the calculation of response-times for tasks with arbitrary activations and deadlines which share resources in multi-core systems scheduled according to the partitioned fixed-priority non-preemptive scheduling. We consider this work an essential building block for the analysis of upcoming multi-core realtime applications where both preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling coexist.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The increasing demand for computational power associated with the rising application complexity in various embedded systems led to a significant interest in multi-core solutions. Strong trends towards multi-core architectures can be observed in communication, media-processing and, more recently, in the automotive applications, where multi-core processors are provided by the semiconductor industry [1], [2]. This trend is also confirmed by the latest specification of the automotive AUTOSAR standard [3].

As multi-core components are planned to be used in realtime applications, formal verification of the timing properties is essential. But timing verification for multi-core systems has been shown as a challenging problem, when shared units are involved [4]. The application of multi-core components introduces a new level of inter-core dependencies that were previously not observed in distributed systems. Even in setups with static task-to-core mapping, the use of physically shared hardware (e.g. shared memory), or synchronization via logical resources (semaphores) introduces dependencies between task executions on different cores, thus challenging the real-time behaviour of the entire system.

To provide the necessary timing guarantees for such systems, various formal scheduling analysis techniques have been proposed that cover partitioned and non-partitioned multiprocessor scheduling with varying degrees of generality. Most of the proposed approaches for multi-core systems consider the problem of preemptive scheduling, while non-preemptive schedulers in multi-core systems received less attention.

Even more, while there are some techniques proposed for the scheduling analysis of tasks which share resources in preemptively scheduled multi-core systems, there is no scheduling analysis solution available for multi-core systems in which tasks that share resources are non-preemptively scheduled.

There are two main reasons why this subject needs more attention. Firstly, non-preemptively scheduled systems are widely used in current real-life applications. For example, most current automotive applications are arbitrated with realtime capable operating systems based on the OSEK/VDX specification [5], which defines priority based preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling and allows resource synchronization via locks administered according to the Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) [5], [6]. The scheduling techniques and the synchronization mechanism from OSEK/VDX have been inherited by the most recent AUTOSAR OS [7] and multi-core OS specifications [3]. Secondly, the current evident evolution of automotive ECUs (Electronic Control Units) towards multi-core architectures will be made by maintaining, as much as possible, the backward compatibility with the current solutions. Thus, non-preemptive tasks as defined by the OSEK/VDX standard will be mapped on multi-core processors possibly sharing common resources with other tasks mapped on the same or on other cores [3]. This is a crucial aspect, as non-preemptive scheduling in single-core processors avoids the synchronization overhead due to resource sharing mechanisms.
This paper addresses non-preemptive multi-core scheduling in several steps:

• We address the AUTOSAR mechanism [3] (i.e. spinlockbased) for inter-core task synchronization in the context of fixed-priority non-preemptive multi-core scheduling and derive corresponding blocking time bounds. • We present an extension to the response-time analysis for single-core non-preemptive scheduling to consider tasks with arbitrary activations and deadlines. • We introduce a response-time analysis for tasks with arbitrary activations and deadlines which share resources in multi-core systems scheduled using partitioned fixedpriority non-preemptive scheduling. Even if global multiprocessor scheduling approaches have received significant attention in the research community, the practical implementation of global schedulers in safety-critical real-time systems, as in automotive applications, has not found its way into practice because of the context switching cost, certification cost in mixed-criticality systems, and not the least, because of the migration cost from legacy OSEK systems. We therefore focus on partitioned multi-core setups, where tasks are statically mapped to the available cores.

Paper organization: In Section II we provide an overview of related work. The system model we use is introduced in Section III. In Section IV we address the AUTOSAR spinlock mechanism in the context of multi-core non-preemptive scheduling and introduce the corresponding blocking time analysis. In Section V we first present an extension to the response-time analysis approach for single-core nonpreemptive scheduling which allows the analysis of arbitrarily activated task sets. After that, we introduce the responsetime analysis approach for arbitrarily activated tasks which share resources in multi-core systems scheduled according to the partitioned fixed-priority non-preemptive scheduling. In Section VI we demonstrate the applicability of the proposed approach. We draw conclusions in Section VII.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Multiprocessor Scheduling. In multiprocessor scheduling, shared resources are often not considered, since traditional multiprocessors used (mostly) local resources.

Multiprocessor scheduling policies can be classified into two different classes, depending on the flexibility of scheduling any given task: the partitioned or the global / nonpartitioned. As explained in the introduction, we will mainly focus on partitioned scheduling where tasks are statically assigned to processors, which are separately scheduled at runtime. The mapping can be done manually (as common in automotive practice) or automatic, e.g. using a bin-packing heuristic [8]. Schedulability tests are then used on each processor to verify whether tasks meet their deadlines.

Different techniques were proposed for schedulability analysis and response time analysis of partitioned multiprocessor systems [9], [10], [4]. While most of the provided analysis solutions consider preemptive scheduling policies in the context of both partitioned and global multiprocessor scheduling, considerable less attention has been given to non-preemptive scheduling policies. In [11] a test condition was proposed for periodic tasks scheduled non-preemptively according to the multiprocessor global EDF policy. In [12] and [13] the authors introduced schedulability test conditions for non-preemptive EDF scheduling and non-preemptive fixed priority scheduling, however, without considering shared resources.
Shared Resources in Multiprocessor Systems. In multicore systems, several cores share resources, such as coprocessors, memories, or memory and peripheral buses.

Shared resources have already been used and investigated for multiprocessors. In [6] the suspension-based locking protocol Multiprocessor Priority Ceiling Protocol (MPCP) was proposed. This protocol assumes that tasks are scheduled according to the partitioned rate monotonic scheduling (RMS) policy and allows to bound the time a task is delayed by other local or remote tasks due to resource contention. The associated schedulability condition needs to be checked for each processor. The spin-based variant of the classic MPCP protocol in [6] was addressed in [14]. In [15] the authors proposed a modified resource control protocol that is similar to MPCP but can also be used together with partitioned EDF. Another shared resource arbitration algorithm is the Multiprocessor Stack Resource Protocol (MSRP) which is compared with MPCP in [16], showing that neither outperforms the other on the complete spectrum of system setups.
Synchronization procedures dedicated to multiprocessor global scheduling were also presented e.g. in [17], however, none of them considers the non-preemptive scheduling.

An empirical evaluation of the performance differences between spin-based and suspension-based synchronization alternatives for multiprocessor systems under different global and partitioned scheduling algorithms was presented in [18], [19]. The results of this evaluation suggest that non-suspending (spin-based) protocols are often a more efficient choice, in particular when critical sections are short and thus the waiting time is less than the cost of blocking and resuming the process. Using improved schedulability algorithms, which consider coordinated approaches for task scheduling, allocation and synchronization, the authors showed in [14] that suspensionbased protocols could in fact behave better than spin-based protocols under low preemptions costs and longer critical sections than those considered in the evaluation in [19].

[20] and [4] introduced a first response-time analysis approach that assumes the partitioned fixed-priority preemptive multiprocessor scheduling, the synchronization protocol MPCP and allows for arbitrary task activations.

Thus, as of today, there is no scheduling analysis solution available for tasks that share resources in non-preemptively scheduled multi-core systems, despite the mentioned practical relevance of that combination. In this paper, we fill this gap by providing a response-time analysis for multi-core systems in this setting. Even more, we address the multi-core nonpreemptive scheduling in the context of current automotive standards, which specify inter-core task synchronization according to the spinlock mechanisms [3]. We consider prior work in the field of uni-processor scheduling, namely the response-time analysis in [21] for non-preemptively scheduled tasks and in [22] for the analysis of CAN (Controller Area Network) messages. In order to capture the inter-core timing dependencies and to calculate tasks' worst-case response times in the presence of dynamic scheduling and shared resources we rely on the system-level analysis procedure presented in detail in [4] and briefly summarized in Section V-C.

div.head: A. Multi-Core System Model
div.p: In this paper, we will focus from now on only on multicore architectures which consist of: (i) a set of m(m ≥ 2) processor cores, each being individually scheduled according to the static priority non-preemptive (SPNP) policy, (ii) a set of shared resources that can be accessed from each of the m cores and (iii) a static set of arbitrarily activated real-time tasks τ = {τ 1 , . . . τ n }. A set of tasks τ p (τ p ∈ τ ) is assumed statically mapped to each core p (p ∈ m), and our goal is to determine the schedulability of the given mapping.

A common priority space across all m cores is assumed and, for simplicity of presentation, each task in this system has a unique static priority indicated by its index -the lowest index is allocated to the highest priority task, i.e. τ 1 .

Each instance of a task τ i , called a job and denoted with J i , is activated by an event, which can be either external (such as interrupts) or the result of another task or bus communication being finished (in which case there is a partial order between the possible task activations). We express task activation patterns with event streams using the upper event arrival function η + i (Δt), and the lower event arrival function η - i (Δt) [23]. These specify the maximum and the minimum number of events that occur in an event stream during any time interval of length Δt. Inversely, event streams can be specified using the functions δ + i (n) and δ - i (n) that represent the largest and smallest time window in which n (n ≥ 2) events can be observed in the stream. The functions η and δ are pseudo-inverse to each other.

Each job of a task τ i is further characterized by its worstcase execution time C i and its (relative) deadline D i , which may be smaller, equal, or larger than the distance to the successive activation. Thus, if a task has a worst-case response time larger than this activation distance, it is possible that another instance of this task may be activated before the previous one has completed. In this case, we assume that new jobs may not start to execute before the previous job is complete, and this queueing time will be considered as part of the job's response time.

Shared resources are assumed to be objects that require serialized access. We distinguish between local (LR) and global resources (GR). Local resources reside on each core and can be accessed only by the tasks that are mapped to it. Global resources are assumed in a separate shared resource module and can be accessed by tasks mapped to different cores. A critical section guarded by a semaphore and protecting a global or a local resource is called global critical section (gcs) or local critical section (lcs). The maximum number of global critical sections that each job J i of a task τ i executes before its completion is n G i , and ω global i represents the maximum duration of such a global critical section. With η+ i→S we denote the load imposed by a task τ i on a shared resource S. Accesses to shared resources are arbitrated according to the synchronization policy introduced in Section IV-A and the shared resource access delays are given solely by the blocking factors derived in Section IV-B.

div.p: It is well known that the overhead due to synchronization mechanisms can be neglected in case of single-processor non-preemptive scheduling. This is ensured by the intrinsic behaviour of the non-preemptive scheduling, which keeps tasks' execution exclusive and therewith also the requests for shared resources. In multi-core setups, this is not the case anymore. Accesses initiated by tasks executing on different cores may interfere as depicted in Fig. 3 where jobs of the tasks τ 1 and τ 5 in the multi-core system in Fig. 1 are blocking each other when requesting the same global shared resource.

As there is no synchronization mechanism for shared resources in multi-core systems which explicitly considers the static priority non-preemptive scheduling, we next introduce a dedicated resource arbitration solution. For this, we consider that a spinlock-based mechanism is used exclusively for intercore synchronization (as proposed in the current AUTOSAR specification [3]) and exploit it in the context of static priority non-preemptive scheduling. This step is needed not only to highlight the impact of sharing resources among cores when assuming the non-preemptive scheduling, but also to ensure the premises for deriving bounded tasks' blocking times and therewith a predictable timing behaviour of multi-core systems in this setting.
We call the arbitration protocol Multi-core Locking Protocol for Non-Preemptive scheduling and use further the abbreviation MLP-NP.

div.head: A. Definition of the MLP-NP Arbitration Policy for Shared Resources in Multi-Core Non-Preemptive Systems
div.p: Tasks priorities. Under static priority non-preemptive scheduling, a job J i of a task τ i which starts executing on its host core will run until completion without any preemption by other local tasks independent of the associated priorities. As tasks under non-preemptive scheduling execute exclusively, priority inversion situations or deadlocks can not occur if nested calls for global resources are forbidden or if a global unique ordering is defined (see below). This makes the use of priority ceilings superfluous. Therefore, a job J i which locks a shared resource (global or local) will execute the associated critical section at the assigned priority.

Arbitration of local shared resources. As a consequence of the local scheduling policy, during the execution of a job J i there will be no pending shared resource requests initiated by other local jobs with J i . Thus, an executing task τ i will always occupy the requested local resources without any blocking by other tasks.

Arbitration of global shared resources. During execution, a job J i of a task τ i which tries to lock a global resource will lock the resource if that is currently not occupied by another remote job. If the requested resource is occupied, the job which has initiated the request will actively wait (spin) until the required resource is released. This means the processor is stalled, and independent of the execution priority no other task mapped on the same core with τ i is allowed to execute. This is imposed by the local non-preemptive scheduler. An example is depicted in Fig. 3 where a job of task τ 2 , which in this case has higher priority than task τ 5 , may not start executing until the active job of task τ 5 completely finishes its execution.

Note that, the AUTOSAR spinlock mechanisms [3] does not explicitly consider the underlying scheduling policy and specify that a higher priority task (e.g. τ 2 ) could preempt a lower priority task (e.g. τ 5 ) during spinning. The nonpreemptive scheduling counters this assumption and imposes larger blocking times on the higher priority tasks.
In case of coinciding requests for a global resource GR i , initiated by jobs of different tasks mapped on different cores, the highest priority job requesting GR i will lock that resource.

Nested calls for shared resources. In order to avoid deadlocks, nested accesses to global resources are not allowed. A job J i which already holds a global resource is not allowed to request another global resource before the previously locked resource has been released. Nested calls with respect to local resources are permitted. Thus, a job holding one global resource may perform calls for local resources and vice-versa, a job holding one or more local resources may perform a call for one global resource.

Other design decisions could be employed for the nesting of global shared resources and for the arbitration of the global shared resources (e.g. FIFO queues for coinciding requests on global shared resources or suspension-based blocking using priority ceilings [6]). If global shared resources shall be nested, an explicit partial ordering of calls for shared resources has to be predefined offline in order to avoid deadlocks and potentially starvation situations (recommended in both, literature [6] and industrial practice [3]). An extended discussion and an evaluation of the trade-offs between the different design decisions regarding the synchronization mechanisms is beyond the scope of this paper.

The MLP-NP arbitration protocol represents a basic solution proposed with the goal of maintaining the compatibility with the non-preemptive scheduling behaviour. In the following, we will derive upper bounds on the blocking times that tasks can experience under MLP-NP. Demonstrating that the blocking time is bounded under all circumstances, we implicitly show that deadlocks are not possible, i.e. that the protocol is safe.

div.head: B. Derivation of Blocking Times
div.p: Next, we derive the worst-case blocking times that arbitrarily activated tasks encounter before completion due to the use of shared resources according to the MLP-NP.

Since task deadlines can be larger than their periods (see Section III-A), the blocking time analysis has to consider the possible influence of overlapping job execution. This influence can be captured by analysing the execution of tasks during their busy interval denoted with w i (q), where q represents the number of activations of a task τ i within w i (q). This analysis will be introduced in detail in Section V-B. For now, assume that we are interested in the blocking time of a task τ i that accesses local and global resources and is activated q times in a time window of size w i (q).
In order to present the blocking factors, the following definitions are introduced 1 :

V. SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS Before presenting our proposed response time analysis approach for tasks which share resources in non-preemptively scheduled multi-core systems we introduce an extension to the response time analysis approach for uni-processor nonpreemptive scheduling in [21], [22] to consider task sets with arbitrary activation patterns (event models).

div.head: A. Response Time Analysis of Arbitrarily Activated Tasks in Uni-Processor Non-Preemptively Scheduled Systems
div.p: The worst-case response time of a fixed priority task τ i on a non-preemptively scheduled single-core processor occurs for a job J i of task τ i within the maximum priority leveli busy period [26], where the maximum busy period (called also busy window) is considered as starting at the so called critical instant [27]. In case of non-preemptive scheduling the critical instant is the moment just after the job J j of a task τ j with the longest core execution time C j among all local tasks with lower priority than τ i starts executing and where job J i is released simultaneously with all higher priority local jobs [21], [22].

div.head: B. Response Time Analysis for Multi-Core Non-Preemptive Scheduling
div.p: Relying on the system model introduced in Section III and on the background provided by the analysis approach for single-core non-preemptive systems discussed in Section V-A, we next introduce a response time analysis approach for non-preemptively scheduled tasks in multi-core systems with shared resources.

For this, two important aspects need to be considered. Firstly, in single-core non-preemptive setups the influence of sharing resources can be neglected due to the intrinsic behaviour of the non-preemptive scheduler which avoids the synchronization overhead due to resource sharing mechanisms. In multi-core systems this is not the case anymore. The blocking times that tasks will experience due to conflicting accesses for shared resources have to be computed and considered when deriving response times bounds.

Secondly, the critical instant scenario must be revisited. It is known that the use of global shared resources may lead to suspension of tasks which possibly defers the tasks' execution times and thus counters the assumptions regarding the critical instant scenario on which the classical response time analysis approach rely (see [6]). This aspect, which was identified in case of sharing resources under multiprocessor static-priority preemptive scheduling, will be now investigated for the case of sharing resources under multiprocessor static-priority nonpreemptive scheduling.

Critical instant. If global resources are not shared between tasks mapped on different cores, the response time analysis problem reduces to the classical approach discussed in Section V-A. There, a task τ i experiences the critical instant scenario, which leads to the worst-case response time, when it is released (i) at the time moment just after a job of a lower priority local task τ j ∈ lpl(i) has started its local execution and (ii) simultaneously with jobs of all higher priority local tasks (tasks ∈ hpl(i)). These arguments also hold when resources are shared between tasks mapped on different cores. Relying on the resource arbitration policy introduced in Section IV-A a task which has an outstanding request for a shared resource will actively wait for that resource without any preemption by other local tasks. This means that the blocking times due to the waiting for shared resources represent an extension of the task's core execution time. Thus, in case of inter-core synchronization mechanisms and core local non-preemptive scheduling, for any job there can not be any higher priority local job that can suspend itself when waiting for a global shared resource. Therefore the effect of deferred execution [6] does not counter the assumptions regarding the critical instant scenario.

div.p: A job J j of a task τ j with lower priority than τ i will start its execution on its host core and will possibly request and even lock required shared resources only when there is no other previously released and unfinished job of a task with priority higher than τ j . Thus, a task τ j can delay the execution of a higher priority local task τ i only if it starts executing before the release time of task τ i and before the release of any other local task with priority higher than i.

From the perspective of the higher priority local tasks, similar to the single-core analysis approach, these will cause the largest possible delay for a local task τ i if they are released simultaneously with task τ i .

The critical instant for a task τ i under partitioned staticpriority non-preemptive multi-core scheduling is represented in Fig. 5 where task τ i is activated at the same moment with the higher priority tasks τ hp1 and τ hp2 just after the lower priority task τ lp has started its execution. The terms BT in Fig. 5 represent the blocking times that different jobs running on a core may experience when the requested global shared resources are locked by jobs of the remote tasks.

Busy Window. Similar to the analysis for uni-processor static priority non-preemptive scheduling the worst-case response time of a task τ i non-preemptively scheduled in multicore systems with shared resources is given by the largest response time of any of the q (q = 0 . . . Q i -1) task activations that lie within the level-i busy window.

Assuming the critical instant scenario under non-preemptive scheduling in a multi-core setup, the level-i busy window of a task τ i consists not only of the time intervals during which the tasks contributing to the busy window execute but also of the time intervals these tasks are blocked and have to wait for the required global shared resources (see Fig. 5). According to the blocking time analysis introduced in Section IV-B the blocking time of a task in multi-core systems with global shared resources is a function of the window size during which the task initiates requests to the required shared resources.
Thus, the length of the level-i busy window of a task τ i in a multi-core system is composed of:

• the longest possible initial blocking (denoted with B i ) caused by one instance of a lower priority local task due to the non-preemptive scheduling behaviour. In case of multi-core setups, the initial blocking time caused by one of the lower priority local tasks is composed of the task's core execution time plus the blocking time when waiting for global shared resources. This is given by:

Thus, the iterative calculation has to be stopped if the "effective" core utilization level (composed of the tasks' core execution times and blocking times) exceeds 100% at some iteration point. In that case the task set is considered unschedulable.

In case of multi-core systems the computation of w i (q) has to consider the blocking times of the tasks when waiting for global shared resources. Thus, w i (q) has to be computed using the following recursive equation:

Similar to equation ( 13), the recurrence relation ( 14) can be solved by iteration, because all components grow with the window size [4]. The recurrence starts with a value of w 0 i (q) = q • C i and ends when w n+1 i (q) = w n i (q), or when the value w n i (q) at some iteration point is so large that the obtained response time r i for the current considered activation q already exceeds τ i 's deadline, in which case the task is unschedulable.

Finally, if worst-case response time values R i have been obtained for all the tasks in the multi-core system, the schedulability test consists of checking whether the condition R i ≤ D i holds for every task τ i .

div.head: C. System-Level Analysis for Multi-Core Systems with Shared Resources
div.p: The response time of a task is in general a function of the activating event model η. But, as can be observed from equation ( 13), ( 14) and (1) -and as illustrated in Fig. 6 the length of the busy windows and the tasks' response times in multi-core systems with shared resources depend also on the delay caused by the use of shared resources, i.e. the response time R i is a function of blocking time B i . This delay in turn depends on the amount of traffic imposed on the shared resources by other tasks on other processors ηj (as shown in Section IV-B), which in turn is a function of the respective local load η j . This translates into a dependency

In order to avoid these dependencies, the shared resource request bound in (1) can be replaced by the bound in (2) which is independent of the task's response time.

A further issue is that tasks' activating event models η can not trivially be bounded in event driven multiprocessor systems where tasks' activations may be the result of other tasks finishing or data arriving over a bus. This problem can be addressed as proposed in [4] by embedding the response time analysis and the blocking time analysis into a compositional analysis approach [28], [23]. Thus, the approach that we propose in this paper was integrated in the compositional system-level iterative analysis flow as follows:

1) Given a set of task activating event models η + for each task in the system, a set of shared resource access event models η+ is derived according to e.g. equation ( 2). 2) Based on the shared resource access event models per core, the shared resource access delays B can in the case of MLP-NP be computed for each task with equations ( 4) and ( 5) (see Section IV-B).

3) The respective blocking times then become part of the response time analysis (see Section V-B) of each task on each core (following equation ( 14)), from which the updated output event models η can be derived. The process is repeated as long as any event model estimate has been refined. The iterative analysis represents a fixed-point problem. Given the monotonicity of the proposed analysis procedure [4] the analysis will either converge (i.e. all task activating event models η + and all shared resource request bounds η+ have not changed after an iteration) towards a fixed point, which represent a conservative solution, or the analysis will be stopped as soon as a real-time constraint is violated.

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTS AND DISCUSSION
div.p: In this section we demonstrate the applicability of the proposed approach by analysing a set of pseudo-randomly generated test cases. For the multi-core system depicted in Fig. 1 we generated test cases such that: on each core we assumed 50% utilization; each task on a core was assigned a random utilization that all add to 50%; the periods of the tasks were generated randomly between 100ms and 1000ms; based on the chosen periods the tasks' worst-case execution times (WCETs) C i were calculated to match their utilizations. Furthermore, in order to deviate from the periodic assumptions, each task was randomly assigned an input jitter from the interval [0, 2 • P i ] (i.e. each task could potentially be activated by a maximum burst of 3 simultaneous activations).

Experiment 1: No nested critical sections. In a first set of experiments we applied the proposed response-time analysis method to multiple test cases (i.e. we generated systems until we got 1000 schedulable configurations) randomly generated as indicated above. We assumed the local resources as exclusively used by the tasks mapped on the same core (i.e. local critical sections are not nestable). Therefore, the time that tasks spend executing local critical sections was considered part of the WCETs. The number of global critical sections was assumed constant for all tasks, being in this case 2. For each test case we varied the length of the tasks' global critical sections from 1% to 25% of their WCETs. The minimum distance between requests d srr (in eq. ( 2)) of each task τ i was set up to be d srr = (C i -0.2ω global i ), i.e. tasks access the global shared resources at the beginning and at the end of their WCETs C i .

Fig. 7a) and b) depicts the WCRTs depending on the critical sections' length for systems with strict periodic tasks and for systems with bursty task activations. For each task the average WCRT over the 1000 setups per critical section length is given. As expected, increasing the size of the critical sections led to increased blocking times and thus to increased response time values. The impact of non-preemptive scheduling and blocking is significant for all the tasks in the system. From the perspective of each task, the increased critical sections length causes an increased delay not only on its own execution but also on the execution of the lower and of the higher priority local tasks. These delays are also parts of the tasks' WCRTs. As illustrated in Fig. 7b) in case of bursty task activations there is an over-proportional growth of the WCRTs. The growth is more evident for the tasks with the lowest priority in the system, i.e. tasks τ 5 and τ 6 . These tasks are strongly affected by the bursty activations of the higher priority local tasks. Depending on the tasks deadlines such an increase may eventually lead to deadline misses.

In order to highlight the individual contribution of different factors to the tasks WCRTs we provide in Fig. 8a) the results for one particular test case configuration (see Table I) and critical sections 5%, 15%, and 25%.

Worth to mention here is the influence of the blocking times on the cores' utilization levels. In case of non-preemptive scheduling the blocking times behave like an extension of the tasks' execution times and thus contribute to the core utilization. But the blocking times of a task actually depend on the execution of other tasks mapped on other cores using the same shared resources. This makes the core utilization a function of the critical section lengths of the other tasks on the other cores. As depicted in Fig. 8b) the "effective" utilization level of the cores increases with the length of the critical sections being at least 10% higher than the normal utilization when the length of the critical sections is 5% of the tasks WCETs, and rising up to 96% in case of Core 2 when the critical sections are 25% of the tasks WCETs.

The tests (non-optimized code) were performed on an Intel Core i5 M460 CPU @ 2.53GHz, 4GB RAM, 64bit Windows and took in average 310ms for systems with purely periodic tasks and 1,8 seconds for systems with bursty task activations. ). The time the tasks spend executing the two local critical sections was considered to be 2% of the task WCET C i .

Under these assumptions, the local resources are further exclusively used by the tasks mapped on the same core. However, the inter-core blocking increases because each time a task τ i is waiting for a global resource, currently locked by a remote task τ j , it will be blocked not only for the duration of the global critical section of τ j but also for the duration of the τ j 's local critical sections. Thus, the tasks' WCRTs increased in comparison to the previous experiments where the nesting of local resource was forbidden (see Fig. 9). Furthermore, the "effective" utilization level of all the cores also increased, rising up to 98% in case of Core 2 when the size of the global critical sections was 25% of the WCETs C i .

Hence, when implementing non-preemptive scheduling on multi-core systems the effect of sharing resources on response times and cores' utilization levels can not be neglected anymore. While in single-core implementations non-preemptive scheduling policies are advantageous by reducing context switching cost where response times are not critical, multi-core setups show an increased load which threatens schedulability beyond deadline violations. This effect constrains the migration of non-preemptive tasks sets from single-core to multicore systems. The analysis we have presented in this paper allows the derivation of tasks' blocking and response times and can be used to guide the designers decisions regarding the implementation and the mapping of applications on multi-core this paper, we addressed the partitioned static-priority non-preemptive multi-core scheduling of tasks with shared resources and arbitrary activations and deadlines, a combination which covers the scheduling strategies of the upcoming automotive multi-core processors using AUTOSAR. We have investigated the effects of mapping non-preemptive staticpriority scheduled task sets from single-core to partitioned multi-core implementation using spin-locking, as it can be derived from the new AUTOSAR multi-core extensions [3]. Here, remote blocking increases utilization, an effect that is unknown in single-core non-preemptive solutions. For that purpose we have developed a new response time analysis approach which incorporates the blocking times that nonpreemptively scheduled tasks may experience when sharing resources in multi-core systems. The results highlight a significant effect that threatens schedulability and suggest the minimization of critical sections in non-preemptive task sets. This work represents an essential building block for the analysis of complex multi-core real-time applications where both preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling will coexist.
